lessons.title: Basic financial concepts and bookkeeping
lessons.html:
The farm as a business

A farm is a business that converts land, labour, capital and management into products for sale. Financial management is about knowing where money comes from, where it goes, what the business owns and owes, and whether it is making a profit. At N4 level the focus is on the foundation: the terms, the source documents and the basic books.

Key terms

  • Income – money earned from sales of crops, animals, milk, services or other sources.
  • Expenses – costs of running the farm: seed, fertiliser, feed, fuel, wages, repairs, interest.
  • Profit or loss – income minus expenses over a period.
  • Assets – what the business owns: land, buildings, machinery, livestock, stock of inputs, cash and money owed by debtors.
  • Liabilities – what the business owes: loans, overdrafts, amounts owed to creditors such as the co-op.
  • Owner's equity – assets minus liabilities: the owner's share of the business.

Source documents

Every transaction should be supported by a document: invoices from suppliers, receipts, sales slips or auction statements, bank statements, payslips, delivery notes. Keep them filed in date order; they are the evidence for the books and for SARS.

The cash book

The simplest record is a cash book (or a cash analysis book) with income on one side and payments on the other, analysed into columns.

DateDetailsFeedFuelWagesTotal
02/03Co-op invoice 4411R8,400R8,400
05/03DieselR3,150R3,150
07/03Weekly wagesR12,600R12,600

The analysis columns let the manager see at a glance how much was spent on each cost item. Reconcile the cash book with the bank statement each month to catch errors and missing entries.

lessons.title: Income statement, balance sheet and cash control
lessons.html:
The income statement

The income statement (profit and loss statement) summarises income and expenses for a period, usually a financial year. A simple layout:

ItemAmount
Sales: weanersR620,000
Sales: maizeR480,000
Total incomeR1,100,000
Direct costs (feed, seed, fertiliser, veterinary, fuel)R540,000
Overhead costs (permanent wages, insurance, repairs, depreciation)R330,000
InterestR60,000
Net farm profitR170,000

Note that depreciation is included as an expense. It spreads the cost of a long-lasting asset, such as a tractor, over its useful life, even though no cash is paid each year.

The balance sheet

The balance sheet shows the financial position on one date. It lists assets and liabilities and the owner's equity. The basic equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity

Assets and liabilities are usually split into current (within 12 months, such as cash, stock, overdraft), and fixed or long-term (land, machinery, mortgage bonds). A growing owner's equity over the years shows that the business is building wealth.

Profit is not cash

A farm can be profitable but still run out of cash, for example when crops are sold months after input costs are paid. Simple cash control measures:

  • Record every payment and receipt promptly.
  • Pay bills on time but not early unless there is a discount.
  • Follow up money owed by buyers.
  • Keep personal and business spending separate.
  • Plan for big seasonal payments such as planting inputs and annual insurance.

Key points

  • Income minus expenses gives profit or loss for a period.
  • Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity.
  • Keep source documents for every transaction and reconcile the cash book monthly.
  • Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life.
  • Profit is not the same as cash; plan for seasonal cash needs.
